title: CORS & Cookie Security
subtitle: What CORS actually does, common misconfigurations that break security, and cookie security patterns for SPAs

content.text: The Same-Origin Policy blocks JavaScript from reading cross-origin responses. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the mechanism that lets a server say 'it's OK for other origins to read my responses'. Servers opt into it via response headers. CORS is not a security feature — it's a way to selectively relax a security feature (SOP). A misconfigured CORS policy can undo the protection SOP provides.

content.filename: How CORS works — the browser flow
content.code:
SIMPLE REQUESTS (GET, POST with safe content types):
  1. Browser sends request with 'Origin: https://myapp.com' header
  2. Server responds with 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.com'
  3. Browser checks: does origin match? Yes → JavaScript can read the response

PREFLIGHT (OPTIONS) — for non-simple requests:
  1. Browser first sends: OPTIONS /api/users with:
       Origin: https://myapp.com
       Access-Control-Request-Method: DELETE
       Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type
  2. Server responds:
       Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.com
       Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, DELETE
       Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type
       Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400  (cache preflight for 24 hours)
  3. If approved: browser sends the actual DELETE request

KEY POINT:
  CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server.
  curl, Postman, and direct server-to-server calls bypass CORS entirely.
  CORS prevents one website from reading another's data in a browser context.
  It does NOT prevent a server from being directly attacked.

content.text: Cookie vs token auth for SPAs

content.code:
OPTION 1: HttpOnly Cookie (recommended for web apps)
  Storage:    Browser sends automatically — not accessible to JS
  CSRF risk:  Yes — mitigated by SameSite=Lax
  XSS risk:   Low — JavaScript can't steal the cookie
  CORS:       Requires credentials: true + specific origin
  Best for:   Traditional web apps, first-party SPAs

OPTION 2: localStorage + Authorization header
  Storage:    Explicitly managed by JavaScript
  CSRF risk:  None — attacker can't read localStorage cross-site
  XSS risk:   HIGH — XSS can read localStorage and steal the token
  CORS:       Just needs Authorization header allowed
  Best for:   Mobile apps, non-browser clients, cross-origin SPAs
  WARNING:    If XSS exists, tokens are stolen and sessions persisted

OPTION 3: sessionStorage
  Like localStorage but cleared when tab closes
  Same XSS risk as localStorage
  Slightly better (token dies with the tab)

OPTION 4: Memory (React state, not stored)
  Most secure against XSS and CSRF
  Lost on page refresh — need refresh token in httpOnly cookie to restore
  Complex to implement

RECOMMENDATION FOR NEW APPS:
  Use HttpOnly + SameSite=Lax cookie for the session
  Use short-lived JWT (15 min) in memory + refresh token in httpOnly cookie
  Never store long-lived tokens in localStorage

questions.question: Your API sets 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' and 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true'. A user on evil.com makes a fetch() to your API with credentials. What happens?
options: The browser allows it — the wildcard grants everyone access
The browser blocks the request — wildcard origin and credentials: true are mutually exclusive in the CORS spec
The server rejects the request because it detects a cross-origin header
The credentials are stripped but the request goes through
questions.explanation: The CORS specification explicitly forbids combining Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. When a browser sees both, it treats the CORS request as failed and blocks JavaScript from reading the response. This is a safeguard — if wildcard + credentials were allowed, any website could read your authenticated users' data. The fix is to use a dynamic origin check (allowlist) instead of the wildcard when credentials are needed. This is a very common misconfiguration that developers hit when building SPAs with cookie-based auth.

faq.q: My React app and API are on different domains. How do I set up cookies?
faq.a: Set your session cookie with SameSite=None; Secure=true (required for cross-site cookies). Configure your API's CORS to specify the React app's exact origin and credentials: true. On the frontend, use fetch() or axios with credentials: 'include'. This is the standard pattern for SPAs on a different domain from their API. Without credentials: 'include', cookies are never sent with cross-origin requests.

examples: In 2018, researchers found that 14.7% of CORS-enabled websites were misconfigured with reflect-origin (trusting any origin). This affected major websites including airlines, banks, and government sites. A single line of JavaScript on a malicious site could read an authenticated user's private data from these APIs

The Portswigger Web Security Academy (labs.portswigger.net) has interactive CORS labs where you can practice exploiting misconfigured CORS policies. This hands-on approach is how security professionals learn to identify and exploit these vulnerabilities in penetration tests
